export function compareRevisions(
  beforeHtml: string,
  afterHtml: string,
): RevisionComparison {
  const before = words(beforeHtml);
  const after = words(afterHtml);
  const beforeCounts = new Map<string, number>();
  for (const word of before) {
    beforeCounts.set(word, (beforeCounts.get(word) ?? 0) + 1);
  }
  let shared = 0;
  for (const word of after) {
    const count = beforeCounts.get(word) ?? 0;
    if (count > 0) {
      shared += 1;
      beforeCounts.set(word, count - 1);
    }
  }
  return {
    wordsBefore: before.length,
    wordsAfter: after.length,
    wordsChanged: before.length + after.length - 2 * shared,
    paragraphsBefore: paragraphs(beforeHtml),
    paragraphsAfter: paragraphs(afterHtml),
  };
}

/**
 * Notes an editor left on a passage that this change rewrote or removed. The
 * link is literal: the note's anchor sentence was in the old passage. That
 * is evidence the change touched what the note was about, not proof that it
 * answered it, and the panel words it that way.
 */
export function notesTouchedBy<T extends { anchor?: string }>(
  change: RevisionPassageChange,
  notes: readonly T[],
): T[] {
  if (!change.before) return [];
  const squash = (text: string) =>
    text.replace(/\s+/g, " ").trim().toLowerCase();
  const before = squash(change.before);
  const after = change.after ? squash(change.after) : "";
  return notes.filter((note) => {
    const anchor = note.anchor ? squash(note.anchor) : "";
    return (
      anchor.length > 12 && before.includes(anchor) && !after.includes(anchor)
    );
  });
}

/**
 * One plain sentence saying what a revision did, from the changes alone: how
 * many passages were rewritten, cut and added, and whose notes the rewrites
 * touched. Written by Twyne so a checkpoint explains itself even when the
 * writer never says what it was for.
 */
export function describeRevision<
  T extends { anchor?: string; personaName: string },
>(changes: readonly RevisionPassageChange[], notes: readonly T[]): string {
  if (!changes.length) return "No change to the text.";
  const rewritten = changes.filter((c) => c.before && c.after).length;
  const cut = changes.filter((c) => c.before && !c.after).length;
  const added = changes.filter((c) => !c.before && c.after).length;
  const n = (count: number, word: string) =>
    `${count} ${word}${count === 1 ? "" : "s"}`;
  const parts = [
    rewritten && `rewrote ${n(rewritten, "passage")}`,
    cut && `cut ${n(cut, "passage")}`,
    added && `added ${n(added, "passage")}`,
  ].filter(Boolean) as string[];
  const said = parts.join(", ").replace(/, ([^,]*)$/, " and $1");
  const editors = [
    ...new Set(
      changes
        .flatMap((c) => notesTouchedBy(c, notes))
        .map((note) => note.personaName),
    ),
  ];
  const touched = editors.length
    ? ` The changes reach passages ${editors.join(", ").replace(/, ([^,]*)$/, " and $1")} had notes on.`
    : "";
  return `${said.charAt(0).toUpperCase()}${said.slice(1)}.${touched}`;
}

/**
 * Return only the passages that differ between two manuscript versions.
 *
 * Exact passages are used as nearby anchors, so inserting one paragraph does
 * not make every paragraph below it look rewritten. The bounded look-ahead
 * keeps comparison linear for long manuscripts while still handling ordinary
 * editorial insertions and removals cleanly.
 */
export function compareRevisionPassages(
  beforeHtml: string,
  afterHtml: string,
): RevisionPassageChange[] {
  const before = passageText(beforeHtml);
  const after = passageText(afterHtml);
  const changes: RevisionPassageChange[] = [];
  const LOOK_AHEAD = 12;
  let beforeIndex = 0;
  let afterIndex = 0;

  while (beforeIndex < before.length || afterIndex < after.length) {
    if (before[beforeIndex] === after[afterIndex]) {
      beforeIndex += 1;
      afterIndex += 1;
      continue;
    }

    if (beforeIndex >= before.length) {
      changes.push({ before: null, after: after[afterIndex++] });
      continue;
    }
    if (afterIndex >= after.length) {
      changes.push({ before: before[beforeIndex++], after: null });
      continue;
    }

    const nextAfterAnchor = findNearby(
      after,
      before[beforeIndex],
      afterIndex,
      LOOK_AHEAD,
    );
    const nextBeforeAnchor = findNearby(
      before,
      after[afterIndex],
      beforeIndex,
      LOOK_AHEAD,
    );

    const afterDistance =
      nextAfterAnchor < 0
        ? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY
        : nextAfterAnchor - afterIndex;
    const beforeDistance =
      nextBeforeAnchor < 0
        ? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY
        : nextBeforeAnchor - beforeIndex;

    if (afterDistance < beforeDistance) {
      changes.push({ before: null, after: after[afterIndex++] });
    } else if (beforeDistance < afterDistance) {
      changes.push({ before: before[beforeIndex++], after: null });
    } else {
      changes.push({
        before: before[beforeIndex++],
        after: after[afterIndex++],
      });
    }
  }

  return changes;
}

# Twyne feedback-card redesign and Sentence Bench refactor

Rollout context: The user asked to improve both persona feedback-card designs, fix Markdown rendering, add an expanded comment view, and make Sentence Bench genuinely useful through multi-model research before implementation.

## Task 1: Persona feedback cards

Outcome: success

Preference signals:
- The user explicitly identified two card types and asked to improve “both,” with the in-passing Markdown issue and requested-card header overflow fixed.
- The user clarified that “live view” meant “an expanded view for the comments that should open up,” indicating they wanted a usable full-comment interaction, not a developer preview.
- The user requested Opus at medium effort for the implementation.

Key steps:
- Inspected `personas-panel.tsx`, shared Markdown rendering, and card styles.
- Delegated implementation to Claude Opus 5.5 at medium effort while preserving unrelated dirty work.
- Reworked shared Markdown parsing, both card presentations, responsive headers, and an accessible expanded dialog.

Reusable knowledge:
- The Markdown bug was in `src/utils/markdown.ts`: escaping the complete input before parsing broke blockquotes and double-escaped code/link content. Parsing first with `marked`, escaping raw HTML through the renderer, sanitizing URLs, and rendering remote images as safe links fixed the issue across all feedback paths.
- Requested cards now use a paper-sheet treatment with a top accent; in-passing notes retain a lighter margin-note treatment without reduced opacity. Long names clamp to two lines, and narrow layouts move the type/tools row below the name.
- Both card types open the same full-note dialog containing author/context, anchor, full Markdown, replies, read-aloud, and actions. Close, Escape, outside click, and focus restoration were verified.

Failures and how to do differently:
- Validation used headless Playwright rather than T3 preview because the preview was unavailable/problematic. Dark theme, screen-reader behavior, and the full test/e2e suites remained unverified.
- The checkout already contained many unrelated dirty changes; future work must preserve them and inspect diffs carefully.

References:
- `src/components/personas/personas-panel.tsx`
- `src/utils/markdown.ts`
- `src/utils/markdown.test.ts`
- `src/utils/personas-markdown-wiring.test.ts`
- Focused validation: `bun test src/utils/markdown.test.ts src/utils/personas-markdown-wiring.test.ts` → 24 pass, 0 fail.
- Browser evidence: `/tmp/twyne-cards/`, dev server `http://127.0.0.1:5174`.

## Task 2: Sentence Bench research and implementation

Outcome: partial

Preference signals:
- The user said they “still can’t see myself using it,” and requested Astra at max, Fable 5.1, and Opus at high to research and challenge one another before implementation. This indicates they value product usefulness over superficial UI polishing and prefer independent research plus critique before coding.
- The user wanted a separate Opus medium agent to implement the converged direction.

Key steps:
- Three models independently analyzed the existing Sentence Bench, then cross-critiqued each other.
- The research rejected the existing rewrite/word/thesaurus/place picker as a generic alternative generator that lacks diagnosis and often has no revision history on cold start.
- The converged workflow became “Compare a revision”: explicitly select one sentence, preserve the original, edit a trial in context, inspect literal changes, optionally request grounded meaning observations, then apply or discard.
- Opus medium implemented the redesign without touching persona-card or shared comment infrastructure.

Reusable knowledge:
- Sentence history is in memory and commonly empty after reload, so history-dependent contested-span/version-stack designs are not suitable as the primary workflow.
- The new flow preserves the exact selection, refuses ambiguous multi-sentence/cross-paragraph selections instead of silently narrowing, shows paragraph context, allows fragments and multiple replacement sentences, and keeps grammar advisory rather than blocking writer-authored text.
- “Read the difference” is explicit and optional, uses the configured prose provider, returns up to two observations with verbatim original/trial/context quotes, validates those quotes in code, invalidates results when inputs change, and never rewrites, ranks, or claims semantic certainty.
- Applying is a single undoable edit with stale-source protection and focus restoration. The old Rewrite/Words/Place tabs, generated and regex candidates, thesaurus, placement panel, comparison panel, meaning probabilities, and automatic opening paths were removed from this surface.

Failures and how to do differently:
- Real model quality and product usefulness were not validated. Browser tests used mocked provider responses; the central hypothesis remains whether grounded semantic readings add enough beyond ordinary editing, diffing, and Undo.
- Hosted users without a configured prose provider cannot use the reading feature because no hosted route was added.
- Recorded film/manual screenshots still contain old Sentence Bench UI in some places; this was documented rather than fully regenerated.
- The provider transport does not abort requests; stale responses are discarded instead.

- Research references included ABScribe (`https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.00117`), Co-Writing with AI on Human Terms (`https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12488`), and Flower et al. (`https://doi.org/10.2307/357381`).

70:- when reviewing Sentence Bench, the user required “one coherent minimum workflow, not a feature bundle” with cold start, Undo parity, semantic uncertainty, writer ownership, removal scope, and acceptance tests -> state what is removed as clearly as what is retained. [Task 2]
71:
72:## Reusable knowledge
73:
74:- In `src/utils/markdown.ts`, parse with `marked` before renderer-level raw-HTML escaping; sanitize links to `http:`, `https:`, and `mailto:`, and render remote images as safe links. Escaping the whole input first breaks `>` blockquotes and double-escapes code/links. [Task 1]
75:- Both card types share an expanded full-note dialog with context, replies, read-aloud, actions, Escape/outside-click close, and focus restoration. Requested cards are paper-sheet styled; in-passing notes are lighter margin notes without reduced opacity; intrinsic headers wrap responsively. [Task 1]
76:- Sentence history commonly disappears on reload, so history-dependent version-stack designs cannot be the cold start. Use `Compare a revision`: exact selection, fixed original, editable trial, paragraph context, literal diff, optional configured-provider reading, then Use revision or Keep original. [Task 2]
77:- Meaning observations are advisory: cap at two, quote exact original/trial/context text, validate in code, and invalidate on input change. Do not add generated rewrites, ranking, safety scores, Jev fallback, or tiny-model semantic authority. Refuse ambiguous selections; allow fragments/multiple replacement sentences with grammar advisory. Apply must protect stale source/unsafe formatting, make one undo step, and restore focus. [Task 2]

53:- The converged workflow became “Compare a revision”: explicitly select one sentence, preserve the original, edit a trial in context, inspect literal changes, optionally request grounded meaning observations, then apply or discard.
54:- Opus medium implemented the redesign without touching persona-card or shared comment infrastructure.
55:
56:Reusable knowledge:
57:- Sentence history is in memory and commonly empty after reload, so history-dependent contested-span/version-stack designs are not suitable as the primary workflow.
58:- The new flow preserves the exact selection, refuses ambiguous multi-sentence/cross-paragraph selections instead of silently narrowing, shows paragraph context, allows fragments and multiple replacement sentences, and keeps grammar advisory rather than blocking writer-authored text.
59:- “Read the difference” is explicit and optional, uses the configured prose provider, returns up to two observations with verbatim original/trial/context quotes, validates those quotes in code, invalidates results when inputs change, and never rewrites, ranks, or claims semantic certainty.
60:- Applying is a single undoable edit with stale-source protection and focus restoration. The old Rewrite/Words/Place tabs, generated and regex candidates, thesaurus, placement panel, comparison panel, meaning probabilities, and automatic opening paths were removed from this surface.
61:
62:Failures and how to do differently:
63:- Real model quality and product usefulness were not validated. Browser tests used mocked provider responses; the central hypothesis remains whether grounded semantic readings add enough beyond ordinary editing, diffing, and Undo.
